analysis.one_liner: Sets a nationwide deadline for investors to sue over securities fraud: five years from the fraud or two years from discovering it.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, with 14 cosponsors, never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Banking Committee after one subcommittee hearing and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When someone is defrauded buying or selling stocks and bonds, courts apply a deadline for suing. This bill would set one uniform federal rule nationwide: an investor could sue within five years of the fraud, or within two years of discovering it — whichever comes later. It would also apply that longer deadline to lawsuits already in court and let investors whose cases had just been thrown out as too late refile them within 60 days. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held a single subcommittee hearing, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who were cheated — especially small investors who often don't discover the fraud until long after it happened. A lawsuit filed years later is often the only way to recover losses from securities fraud, so a longer, uniform deadline directly affects their chance to get money back. People whose cases were dismissed shortly before the bill as filed too late could refile within 60 days.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a nationwide deadline of the later of five years from the violation or two years from when the investor discovered it through reasonable diligence [S2] [S3].
Applies the new, longer deadline to all proceedings pending on or after June 19, 1991 [S3].
Lets investors whose cases were dismissed as filed too late after June 19, 1991 refile within 60 days of enactment, if those cases would have been timely under both the old law and the new rule [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Securities firms, public companies, their auditors, and their insurers would face a longer window during which they can be sued for fraud, including a 60-day wave of revived cases dismissed just before the bill. An outside five-year limit also gives them certainty that claims older than that cannot be brought.

drawbacks.text: A federal outside limit of five years would cut off some claims that state law would have allowed longer to bring — investors in states with longer deadlines would lose part of their ability to sue [S3].
Applying the new rule to cases already in court and reopening dismissed cases would revive litigation on old transactions, where evidence and witnesses are harder for both sides to reconstruct [S3].

Setting one national deadline does give securities firms and companies a predictable, uniform cutoff instead of a patchwork of state rules, which is the main good-faith argument for a shorter, fixed clock [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For investors the gain is substantial: frauds are often discovered years after the fact, and a 'later of' discovery rule plus a 60-day refile window directly protects people whose cases were just thrown out. The costs fall mainly on the securities industry as longer legal exposure, not on the public; the main real cost to investors is that five years becomes an outside cap even where state law was more generous. On balance the bill favors defrauded investors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held one subcommittee hearing on securities issues in October 1991, but the committee never voted it out and the Senate never took it up before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Bryan introduced the bill on July 23, 1991, with six original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1] [S3] [S5].
Fourteen senators cosponsored it — 10 Democrats and 4 Republicans [S4].
The Banking Committee's Subcommittee on Securities held hearings on October 2, 1991 [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill was never reported out of committee and never received a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities firms, public companies, and auditors who would have faced a longer window for investor fraud suits — plus investors whose dismissed cases stayed dismissed, since the 60-day refile window never came into being.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brokerages and issuers facing fraud suits

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: Sen. Bryan (D-NV) recruited original cosponsors from both parties, and the 14 cosponsors split 10 Democrats and 4 Republicans; the bill died in committee without a roll-call vote.

industries.industry: Securities industry (brokerage firms and public companies as fraud defendants)
industries.note: The bill would extend how long defrauded investors can sue them, and revive cases dismissed as too late. A longer liability window is a direct cost to the industry and the main protection for investors.
Auditors are frequent defendants in securities fraud suits, so a longer limitations period extends their legal exposure.
